FirstWARN Forecast
Wednesday, September 9, 2026
Key Weather Headlines
Heat Advisory continues across southeastern and south-central Missouri and southern Illinois through this evening.
Heat index values near or above 105° are possible, especially across southeastern Missouri and southwestern Illinois.
Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms today and tonight, with damaging winds the primary threat.
Showers and thunderstorms become widespread tonight into Thursday morning.
Heavy rainfall is possible, especially along and near the I-70 and I-44 corridors.
Significant rainfall totals of 2 to 3 inches are possible, with isolated amounts of 4 to 5 inches.
Localized minor flooding is possible, although widespread flash flooding is not expected at this time.
Much cooler Thursday, with highs mainly in the upper 70s to lower 80s.

Another hot and increasingly unsettled day is ahead across the region as a cold front slowly pushes southward. The front will bring increasing clouds, showers, and thunderstorms today into tonight, eventually ushering in a much cooler air mass for Thursday. While the heat will remain a concern this afternoon, the bigger weather story will become the thunderstorms and potential for significant rainfall tonight into Thursday morning.

A Heat Advisory remains in effect across portions of southeastern and south-central Missouri and southern Illinois through this evening. Temperatures will climb into the low to middle 90s in areas ahead of the front, with increasing humidity pushing heat index values toward 100 to 105 degrees. The highest confidence in heat index values of 105 degrees or higher is across southeastern Missouri and southwestern Illinois. Increasing clouds and scattered showers could keep temperatures from getting quite as hot in some locations, so exactly how high the heat index gets will vary considerably from place to place.

Farther north, cooler conditions will already begin developing behind the cold front. Northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois could see showers much of the day, with temperatures held in the upper 70s and lower 80s. The front is expected to slow near the I-70 corridor around midday into early afternoon, creating a sharp contrast between the cooler air behind it and the hot, humid air remaining to the south and east.

Thunderstorms Increase Tonight

The threat for thunderstorms will increase considerably this evening as the cold front interacts with a very warm and humid air mass. Storms will become more widespread tonight and continue into Thursday morning.

There is a Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms today and tonight, with the primary concern being strong to damaging wind gusts. Most storms are not expected to become severe, but a stronger storm or two could produce damaging winds, particularly if storms organize into a bowing segment. Large hail and tornadoes are not expected to be the primary concerns with this system.

Heavy Rain Threat

A slow-moving frontal boundary combined with abundant atmospheric moisture will create an environment capable of producing locally heavy rainfall. The atmosphere contains more than two inches of precipitable water, which is quite high for this time of year. Storms will also tend to move along the front rather than quickly clearing the area.

This raises the potential for significant rainfall totals, particularly near and along the I-70 and I-44 corridors. Some areas could receive 2 to 3 inches of rain, with isolated totals potentially reaching 4 to 5 inches through Thursday afternoon.

The good news is that widespread flash flooding is not currently expected. Soil conditions across much of the area are quite dry, and the rainfall should generally occur over several hours rather than all falling in a short period. Most of this rain should be beneficial, although localized minor flooding of low-lying areas, poor drainage locations, and smaller streams will be possible.

Rainfall amounts will vary considerably over a relatively short distance. One community could receive several inches while another nearby location sees considerably less.

Thursday Brings a Dramatic Change

Showers and thunderstorms will continue into Thursday morning, with some lingering precipitation possible into Thursday afternoon. Clouds, rain, and the passage of the cold front will bring a dramatic temperature change.

High temperatures Thursday will generally remain in the upper 70s to lower 80s, a stark contrast to the heat we've experienced this week.

The exact timing of the end of the rain remains somewhat uncertain. Most guidance suggests precipitation will gradually diminish Thursday afternoon or evening, although a few slower solutions keep showers and a few thunderstorms around into Friday morning, especially across southeastern Missouri and southwestern Illinois.

Friday Through Early Next Week

The cooler weather will be relatively brief. Friday should bring more sunshine and temperatures returning to the 80s.

The weekend and early next week will feature a somewhat unsettled pattern as several upper-level disturbances move across the region and a frontal boundary wavers between the Midwest and Mid-Mississippi Valley. This means there will be several opportunities for showers and thunderstorms, particularly Friday night into Saturday and again Monday night into Tuesday.

However, this does not look like a continuous stretch of wet weather. There should be plenty of dry time between disturbances, and not everyone will see rain each day.

Temperatures will generally run above average, with highs mainly in the mid-80s to lower 90s through the weekend and into early next week. There is still considerable uncertainty by Tuesday and beyond depending on where the frontal boundary ultimately settles.

FirstWARN Bottom Line

Today is a day of transition. We begin with dangerous heat, move into an increasingly active thunderstorm pattern this evening, and then turn much cooler Thursday.

The most important things to watch will be heat index values this afternoon, strong thunderstorm wind gusts tonight, and the potential for significant rainfall along the I-70 and I-44 corridors. The rain could be quite beneficial given the recent dryness, but localized flooding will still be possible where thunderstorms repeatedly move over the same areas.

Thursday will feel like a completely different weather pattern, with much cooler temperatures in the upper 70s and lower 80s.
severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

🔴 Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5)

Central Illinois
Areas northeast of Springfield, Illinois
Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

🟤 Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5)

Northeast Missouri
Central Missouri
Eastern Missouri
St. Louis Metro
West-central Illinois
Southwest Illinois

🟡 Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5)

Southern Missouri
South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

🟢 Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5)

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.

First Warn Weather: First. Accurate. Trusted.
